component_claim: Skill format & progressive disclosure (3-level metadata->body->bundled files)
title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
org_author: Anthropic (Barry Zhang, Keith Lazuka, Mahesh Murag)
quote_or_paraphrase: "At startup, the agent pre-loads the name and description of every installed skill into its system prompt." Because the skill's body and bundled files are read only when needed rather than all at once: "the amount of context that can be bundled into a skill is effectively unbounded."
caveats: Anthropic-specific product description (Claude/Claude Code); describes the mechanism our SKILL.md discovery layer reuses, not a routing-to-subagent composition. The 'effectively unbounded' claim is about the content bundled within a single skill (because it need not be read into context up front), not about the number of skills that can be installed; every installed skill's name/description metadata still loads into the system prompt at startup, which is a real (if typically small) per-skill cost.

component_claim: SKILL.md frontmatter spec (name/description/allowed-tools) as portable format
title: Specification - Agent Skills (open spec)
org_author: Agent Skills open-spec maintainers (agentskills.io; originated at Anthropic)
pub_date: Accessed 2026-07-28 (spec published 2025-12-18 per Anthropic update note)
quote_or_paraphrase: "A skill is a directory containing, at minimum, a SKILL.md file... allowed-tools: Space-separated string of pre-approved tools the skill may use. (Experimental)"
caveats: Confirms the discovery-layer format is a cross-vendor open spec, not unique to any one product; 'allowed-tools' is explicitly marked experimental.

component_claim: Subagent isolated context window, tool restriction, and model-cost routing
title: Create custom subagents
quote_or_paraphrase: "Each subagent runs in its own context window with a custom system prompt, specific tool access, and independent permissions... Control costs by routing tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku."
caveats: Describes Claude Code's own subagent feature, not a skill-triggered subagent composition specifically; explicitly names 'faster, cheaper models like Haiku' as a stated benefit.

component_claim: When to delegate to a subagent (research-heavy, parallel, fresh-perspective, pipeline tasks)
title: How and when to use subagents in Claude Code
quote_or_paraphrase: "A subagent is an isolated Claude instance with its own context window. It takes a task, does the work, and returns only the result... Multiple subagents can run in parallel, and each can have different permissions."
caveats: Practical guidance for Claude Code; does not address routing from a Skill specifically, nor cross-model-family (e.g., GPT parent + Claude specialist) composition.

component_claim: Explicit product-level distinction between Skills (dynamically-loaded instructions/resources) and Subagents (context-isolated task workers)
title: Skills explained: How Skills compares to prompts, Projects, MCP, and more
quote_or_paraphrase: "Skills are folders containing instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude discovers and loads dynamically when relevant to a task... Skills use progressive disclosure: metadata loads first (~100 tokens)..." contrasted in the same guide with: "Subagents are specialized AI assistants with their own context windows, custom system prompts, and specific tool permissions... subagents handle discrete tasks independently and return results to the main agent."
caveats: Confirms Skills and Subagents are documented by Anthropic as two distinct, separately-named mechanisms; the composition of one triggering the other is left to the reader/implementer, not specified here. Both quotes verified verbatim against the live page on 2026-07-28.

component_claim: Custom agent invoked as an isolated sub-agent by the parent runtime, with scoped tools
title: Custom agents and sub-agent orchestration
quote_or_paraphrase: "When a user's request matches an agent's expertise, the Copilot runtime automatically delegates to that agent as a sub-agent-running it in an isolated context while streaming lifecycle events back to the parent session." Example agents each declare a distinct, narrow `tools` allowlist (e.g. `["grep","glob","view"]`).
caveats: This is the SDK-level mechanism GitHub Copilot itself uses for custom/sub-agents; the shown example snippet does not set a different `model` per agent, but the same page's configuration reference documents a `model` field and a `skills` field for exactly this purpose - see evidence.csv row 29.

component_claim: Copilot CLI: model may delegate to a custom agent (subagent) at its own judgment; agent profiles define tools/instructions
title: Invoking custom agents (Copilot CLI)
quote_or_paraphrase: "The AI model being used by the CLI can choose to delegate a task to a subsidiary subagent process, that operates using a custom agent with specific expertise, if it judges that this would result in the work being completed more effectively." Built-in agents include Explore, Task, General-purpose, Code-review.
caveats: This is the exact CLI surface referenced by the target reference implementation; confirms delegation is model-judgment-based, matching the 'parent LLM decides to invoke' framing, but says nothing about per-agent model override in this specific page.

component_claim: GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Haiku 4.5 are both GA models selectable in GitHub Copilot
title: Supported AI models in GitHub Copilot
quote_or_paraphrase: Table listing 'GPT-5.6 Sol | OpenAI | GA' and 'Claude Haiku 4.5 | Anthropic | GA' among supported Copilot models.
caveats: Availability depends on plan/surface and is explicitly noted as subject to change ('Model availability is subject to change').

component_claim: Measured per-token price gap between GPT-5.6 Sol (parent) and Claude Haiku 4.5 (specialist)
title: Models and pricing for GitHub Copilot
quote_or_paraphrase: GPT-5.6 Sol (Default tier, <=272K input): Input $5.00 / Cached $0.50 / Output $30.00 per 1M tokens. Claude Haiku 4.5: Input $1.00 / Cached $0.10 / Output $5.00 per 1M tokens.
caveats: MEASURED, not inferred: this is a directly quoted, dated vendor price table, giving a verifiable 5x input / 6x output price ratio motivating the 'cheaper model' half of the composition. Prices are subject to change and this is Copilot's usage-based billing rate, not raw provider API pricing.

component_claim: GPT-5.6 Sol positioned as the highest-reasoning, most expensive tier of the GPT-5.6 family
title: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna are now available in GitHub Copilot
quote_or_paraphrase: "GPT-5.6 Sol: The highest reasoning ceiling in the family. Best for complex reasoning over large codebases and demanding, long-running agentic work."
caveats: Confirms Sol's intended role as the 'expensive parent' model but says nothing about pairing it with a specific cheaper specialist model.

component_claim: 'Agents as tools' pattern: manager agent keeps control and calls specialist agents through Agent.as_tool()
title: Agent orchestration
quote_or_paraphrase: "Agents as tools: A manager agent keeps control of the conversation and calls specialist agents through Agent.as_tool(). ... Use agents as tools when a specialist should help with a bounded subtask but should not take over the user-facing conversation."
caveats: Same structural shape (parent retains control, specialist returns a bounded result) but the SDK docs do not frame this as a context-minimization or cost-routing technique specifically; framed mainly as a conversational-ownership choice vs. Handoffs.

component_claim: Handoffs: delegate tasks to another agent, represented as a callable tool
title: Handoffs
quote_or_paraphrase: "Handoffs allow an agent to delegate tasks to another agent... Handoffs are represented as tools to the LLM. So if there's a handoff to an agent named Refund Agent, the tool would be called transfer_to_refund_agent."
caveats: Handoffs transfer ownership of the conversation to the specialist (specialist becomes the active agent), which differs from this repo's pattern where the parent retains control and only receives a compact return.

component_claim: Per-agent `model` field allows assigning a different (cheaper) model to a specialist agent
title: Agents
quote_or_paraphrase: Agent configuration table lists `model` ("Which LLM to use") as a per-agent, optional property, independent of `tools` and `handoffs`.
caveats: Confirms the SDK mechanically supports per-agent model choice, which is a prerequisite for the 'cheaper/smaller model' half of the composition, but the docs page does not itself discuss cost or context-size rationale.

component_claim: Coordinator agent delegates to sub-agents with scoped 'mode' limiting return/interaction behavior
title: Build collaborative agent teams
quote_or_paraphrase: "In a collaborative agent team in ADK, a coordinator agent handles delegation of tasks to one or more subagents... subagents are assigned an operating mode to manage their behavior and limit their scope of work... single_turn: No user interaction with automatic return and can be run in parallel."
caveats: Modes govern interaction/return behavior, not explicitly tool allowlisting or model selection in this page; a coordinator + narrow-scope worker shape, not a skill-triggered discovery layer.

component_claim: Handoff is a multi-agent design pattern originating in OpenAI's experimental 'Swarm' project
title: Handoffs (AutoGen Core design pattern)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Handoff is a multi-agent design pattern introduced by OpenAI in an experimental project called Swarm. The key idea is to let agent delegate tasks to other agents using a special tool call."
caveats: Documents lineage of the general handoff/delegation idea (attributed to OpenAI Swarm), not the specific skill+subagent+model-routing composition; AutoGen's handoff returns control to a topic-based routing agent rather than a single parent. IMPORTANT: this page's own reference implementation is NOT an isolated-context pattern-the handed-off `UserTask` message is defined as `context: List[LLMMessage]`, i.e. it explicitly carries the full running conversation history to the next agent. Do not cite this source as evidence of isolated-context subagents; it should only be cited for handoff/delegation lineage.

component_claim: Handoff orchestration lets agents transfer control based on context/request in Semantic Kernel
title: Handoff Agent Orchestration
quote_or_paraphrase: "Handoff orchestration allows agents to transfer control to one another based on the context or user request. Each agent can 'handoff' the conversation to another agent with the appropriate expertise." Explicitly marked as an experimental Agent Framework feature.
caveats: Feature explicitly labeled experimental/subject to change; a control-transfer handoff model, not a parent-retains-control/compact-return model.

component_claim: Multiagent orchestration is justified only above single-agent-with-tools on a stated complexity ladder
title: AI Agent Orchestration Patterns - Azure Architecture Center
quote_or_paraphrase: "Multiagent orchestration... Adds coordination overhead, latency, and failure modes. You can justify the added complexity because a single agent can't reliably handle certain tasks due to prompt complexity, tool overload, or security requirements."
caveats: General pattern catalog covering sequential/concurrent/group-chat/handoff/magentic patterns; does not name or describe a 'skill discovery -> subagent delegation -> compact return' composition as a distinct catalog entry.

component_claim: LangChain names 'Subagents' and 'Skills' as two separate, explicitly distinguished multi-agent patterns
title: Multi-agent
quote_or_paraphrase: Pattern table: "Subagents: A main agent coordinates subagents as tools... Skills: Specialized prompts and knowledge loaded on-demand. A single agent stays in control while loading context from skills as needed."
caveats: Strong corroboration that the framework literature treats Subagents and Skills as two distinct named patterns rather than one composed pattern; LangChain does not document a named pattern where a Skill triggers a Subagent call.

component_claim: Subagents are stateless, tool-invoked, and provide context isolation from the main conversation
title: Subagents
quote_or_paraphrase: "Subagents are stateless-they don't remember past interactions, with all conversation memory maintained by the main agent. This provides context isolation: each subagent invocation works in a clean context window, preventing context bloat in the main conversation."
caveats: Confirms the 'isolated context, compact return' shape as a named, documented pattern in a major OSS framework, independent of Anthropic/GitHub Copilot.

component_claim: CrewAI agents may delegate tasks to other agents via an `allow_delegation` flag; each agent can use a distinct LLM
title: Agents
quote_or_paraphrase: Agent attribute table: "Allow Delegation (optional) | allow_delegation | bool | Allow the agent to delegate tasks to other agents. Default is False." and "LLM (optional) | llm | ... | Language model that powers the agent."
caveats: Confirms per-agent model assignment and delegation are both native, independently documented primitives in CrewAI, but CrewAI does not document a skill-style progressive-disclosure discovery layer feeding delegation decisions.

component_claim: LLM cascades routing queries to cheaper models can match/beat top-tier model accuracy while cutting cost up to 98%
title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
org_author: Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou (Stanford)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Our experiments show that FrugalGPT can match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% with the same cost."
caveats: Academic support for the general 'route cheap, escalate when needed' cascade idea underlying the cheaper-specialist-model rationale; not about tool scoping, skills, or agent frameworks, and cascade != our single-hop skill-to-subagent delegation.

component_claim: Learned router models can cut LLM serving cost >2x by dynamically choosing between a strong and weak model
title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
org_author: Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, Vincent Wu, Wei-Lin Chiang, Tianhao Wu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, M Waleed Kadous, Ion Stoica (UC Berkeley et al.)
quote_or_paraphrase: "We propose several efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger and a weaker LLM during inference... our approach significantly reduces costs-by over 2 times in certain cases-without compromising the quality of responses."
caveats: Learned-router framing differs from this repo's rule-based Skill-description trigger; still directly relevant academic backing for cost/quality trade-offs of routing between models of different capability tiers.

component_claim: Open-source multi-agent conversation framework where customizable, conversable agents complete tasks together
title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
org_author: Qingyun Wu, Gagan Bansal, Jieyu Zhang, et al. (Microsoft Research et al.)
quote_or_paraphrase: "AutoGen is an open-source framework that allows developers to build LLM applications via multiple agents that can converse with each other to accomplish tasks. AutoGen agents are customizable, conversable, and can operate in various modes that employ combinations of LLMs, human inputs, and tools."
caveats: Foundational academic multi-agent-delegation reference; does not address skill-based progressive-disclosure discovery or per-agent cost-tier routing specifically. Abstract verified via direct fetch of the arXiv abstract page (raw HTML `og:description`), the same method used for FrugalGPT and RouteLLM.

component_claim: Curating the smallest high-signal token set, and avoiding bloated/ambiguous tool sets, is framed as a context-engineering (not primarily safety) concern
title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
quote_or_paraphrase: "One of the most common failure modes we see is bloated tool sets that cover too much functionality or lead to ambiguous decision points about which tool to use... curating a minimal viable set of tools for the agent can also lead to more reliable maintenance and pruning of context over long interactions. Elsewhere: LLMs have an "attention budget" that they draw on when parsing large volumes of context; every new token introduced depletes this budget by some amount."
caveats: This is the clearest first-party framing that tool-set minimization is argued primarily as a context/attention-budget concern; the same blog does not separately quantify the token cost of each unused tool definition, so exact per-tool schema-token savings are not measured here (see Tool Attention row for an attempted external measurement).

component_claim: LLM performance degrades non-uniformly as input length grows, even on simple, controlled tasks ('context rot')
title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
source_type: Independent research report (primary, cited by Anthropic)
quote_or_paraphrase: "We demonstrate that even under these minimal conditions, model performance degrades as input length increases, often in surprising and non-uniform ways... An evaluation across 18 LLMs... revealing nonuniform performance with increasing input length."
caveats: MEASURED empirical result about context length generally; it does not isolate tool-schema tokens specifically as the degrading factor, so using it to justify 'fewer tool schemas' is an inference by analogy, not a direct measurement of tool-count effects.

component_claim: Dynamic tool gating / lazy schema loading proposed to reduce per-turn MCP/tool schema token overhead
title: Tool Attention Is All You Need: Dynamic Tool Gating and Lazy Schema Loading for Eliminating the MCP/Tools Tax in Scalable Agentic Workflows
quote_or_paraphrase: Title and abstract page indicate the paper proposes dynamic tool gating and lazy schema loading to reduce token overhead from large tool/MCP catalogs (full abstract not independently re-verified beyond the arXiv listing page).
caveats: INFERRED, not independently verified in depth: this is a very recent, non-peer-reviewed preprint located via search; it is the closest academic-style source found for 'fewer tool schemas reduces context tokens,' but its findings should be treated as preliminary and unvetted, not established consensus.

component_claim: Practitioners informally report subagent-heavy sessions dominate token/credit spend, and recommend routing planner vs. worker agents to different price tiers
title: Why Claude Code Subagents Burn So Many Tokens
quote_or_paraphrase: "The biggest lever is model routing: planner on Opus, workers on Haiku or Sonnet. Haiku is 5x cheaper than Opus... Route each worker explicitly with the model field in its frontmatter."
caveats: Gray literature; author-compiled pricing table and anecdotes (Reddit/GitHub issue quotes) are not independently audited by us beyond cross-checking the Haiku/Opus price ratio against Anthropic's own published pricing, which is directionally consistent. No canonical/standard name for the composed pattern is used here either.

component_claim: Subagents described informally as a 'team of specialists' with restricted tool access improving both focus and safety
title: A practical guide to subagents in Claude Code
quote_or_paraphrase: "Instead of having one AI trying to do everything, you can assemble a team of specialists." "You control their tool access. You decide which tools each subagent can use. Need an agent that can review code but not touch any files? You can limit its permissions, which adds a nice layer of security and keeps the agent from getting distracted."
caveats: Gray literature summarizing Anthropic's own docs; explicitly conflates the security/least-privilege benefit with the 'keeps the agent from getting distracted' context benefit in the same sentence, illustrating why this repo's report insists on separating the two rationales.

component_claim: GitHub Copilot custom-agent config schema documents a per-agent `model` override and a per-agent `skills` preload on the same agent object, alongside the `tools` allowlist
title: Custom agents and sub-agent orchestration
quote_or_paraphrase: Configuration reference table: "model | string | | Model identifier to use while this agent runs" and "skills | string[] | | Skill names to preload into the agent's context at startup." Body text: "Set `model` and `reasoningEffort` to override the parent session's model settings while a custom agent runs." "Per-agent skills" section: "When specified, the full content of each listed skill is eagerly injected into the agent's context at startup-the agent doesn't need to invoke a skill tool; the instructions are already present. Skills are opt-in: agents receive no skills by default, and sub-agents do not inherit skills from the parent."
caveats: This is the single most direct documented schema found in this research combining a cheaper/different model, a narrow tool allowlist, and skill content on one subagent definition - corrects an earlier draft of this report that stated GitHub's custom-agent docs said nothing about per-agent model override. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the `skills` field is a static list configured by whoever defines the agent, eagerly injecting full skill content at agent-definition time; it is not the relevance-triggered, progressive-disclosure mechanism (metadata loads first, body loads only if triggered) that defines Agent Skills in Anthropic's docs or in GitHub Copilot's own separate 'About agent skills' feature (row 32). No evidence was found that a `customAgents` entry's `skills` list is itself driven by an outer Skill's runtime discovery/trigger decision.

component_claim: Google ADK `task`/`single_turn`-mode subagents run in an isolated session branch and cannot see peer agents' events
title: Build collaborative agent teams
quote_or_paraphrase: "Each `task` or `single-turn` mode agent operates in its own isolated session branch. When these agents operate in parallel, each agent only sees events from its own branch when building context for AI model calls, and cannot see what its peer agents are doing. Once all parallel branches complete, the parent agent receives the collected results and can proceed."
caveats: Corrects an earlier draft of this report that omitted Google ADK from the isolated-context-window prior art list (§4, §8). This isolation is documented specifically for `task` and `single_turn` collaboration modes; ADK's default `chat` mode is a manual, non-isolated hand-off, per the same page's mode-comparison table (evidence.csv row 14).

component_claim: GitHub Copilot documents an Agent Skills mechanism (folders of instructions/scripts/resources loaded when relevant), separate from its custom-agent/subagent mechanism
title: About agent skills
quote_or_paraphrase: "Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot can load when relevant to improve its performance in specialized tasks. The Agent Skills specification is an open standard, used by a range of different AI systems." Skills work with Copilot cloud agent, code review, Copilot CLI, the Copilot app, and agent mode in VS Code/JetBrains. The companion how-to page confirms the same SKILL.md name/description/allowed-tools frontmatter format as the open spec (see https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/add-skills).
caveats: This is the source establishing that GitHub Copilot documents BOTH a Skill-equivalent discovery mechanism (this row) AND a subagent/custom-agent delegation mechanism (rows 7-8) — correcting an earlier draft of this report that stated only Anthropic and LangChain document both halves. GitHub's docs still describe skills and custom agents as two separate features on separate pages; no GitHub source found names a single composed 'skill triggers subagent' pattern.
